lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.unitTitle: Body Signals, Rest, and Fueling Meals
lessonRef.title: Explicit model: noticing without judging

standardsRefs: Ready for Life v1, Grade 4 Unit 4: Body Signals, Rest, and Fueling Meals
objective: Learners catch three real body-signal thoughts as they first occur, rewrite each as a neutral noticing statement with no judging words, then compare one original judging thought against its neutral rewrite side by side and identify the exact word or phrase that turned a plain signal into a judgment.
scenario: When a body signal shows up, it is easy for a thought about it to turn into a judgment, like thinking a signal shouldn't be happening, instead of a plain observation of what the body is doing. Today the learner catches three real body signals, first as the thought actually shows up, then rewrites each one as a neutral, non-judgmental noticing statement.
materials: a quiet moment to think back over the day

tasks.directions: Before you begin noticing today, look at one example of the difference between a judging thought and a noticing statement.

prompts.text: Which of these is a neutral noticing statement instead of a judgment?
choices: My legs feel tired after standing all morning.
I'm being lazy because my legs feel tired.

tasks.directions: Three separate times today, catch a body signal as it happens. First write down the thought exactly as it first showed up in your head. Then rewrite it as a plain, neutral noticing statement that describes only what your body is doing, with no judging words like 'should,' 'lazy,' or 'bad.'

prompts.text: I wrote down my first, unedited thought for at least three signals.
I rewrote each one as a neutral statement describing only what my body is doing.
None of my three rewritten statements contain a judging word like 'should,' 'lazy,' 'bad,' or 'good.'

tasks.directions: Pick the pair, original thought and rewritten noticing statement, where the judging version was strongest, and compare the two versions closely to figure out exactly which word or phrase turned a plain body signal into a judgment.

prompts.text: Write your original judging thought and your rewritten noticing statement side by side for that one pair.
Point to the exact word or phrase in the original that made it a judgment instead of a plain observation, and explain how you knew.

tasks.directions: Think about how it felt to read your neutral version back compared to your first judging thought.

prompts.text: Explain whether the neutral noticing statement changed how you felt about the signal itself, and why noticing without judging might be a useful habit even when a signal is uncomfortable.

remediation: If a learner's 'rewritten' statements still contain judging words dressed up as description (for example calling a signal 'annoying' or 'ridiculous'), reteach with a strike-through exercise: give the learner three judgment-loaded sentences, have them physically cross out every opinion word, and check whether a true, neutral sentence remains once the opinion words are gone.
extension: Have the learner notice one out-loud comment from someone else during the day that sounds like a judgment about a body signal, and privately write how they would rephrase it as a neutral noticing statement, without correcting the other person out loud.
